JUDGMENT OF
GORMAN, P.C. J.

(SENTENCE)

Introduction:

[
1
]     This case is illustrative of the
nature of the intimate partner violence that is inflicted upon women in this
Province on a regular and consistent basis.  Mr. Rowsell struck his intimate
partner (Ms. X) on the head with a golf club, resulting in her bleeding
profusely and causing serious physical and psychological harm to her.  She
escaped the confinement Mr. Rowsell had subjected her to, by jumping out a
window.

[
2
]     After a trial in relation to
this incident (see
[2025] N.J. No. 52 (P.C.)
), Mr. Rowsell was convicted of the
offences of aggravated assault, assault
(two counts),
uttering a threat, unlawful confinement, and breach of a release order (two
counts)
, contrary to
sections 268
,
266
,
264.1(1)
,

279(2)
, and
145(5)
of the
Criminal Code of Canada
, R.S.C. 1985.

[
3
]     In addition, and in relation
to other victims, Mr. Rowsell pleaded guilty to having committed the offences
of uttering a threat (three counts), interfering with the lawful use of
property, breach of a release order, and committing an indecent act, contrary
to
sections 264.1(1)
(a),
430(1)
(c),
145(5)
, and
173(1)

of
the
Criminal Code
. One of the individuals threatened was a police
officer (Constable Salman Anjum).  The threats uttered by Mr. Rowsell to this
officer included numerous vile racial slurs.

The Issue:

[
4
]     The sole issue that I must decide
is what constitutes an appropriate sentence for the offences committed by Mr.
Rowsell.
Because of the nature of the relationship
that existed between Ms. X and
Mr. Rowsell at the time the offences
were committed,
sections
718.2(a)(ii) and
718.201

of the
Criminal Code
apply.  It is well settled that these provisions
mandate that when imposing sentence for offences involving an intimate partner,
that sentencing judges must prioritize the sentencing objectives of denunciation
and deterrence (
see
R. v. Bear
,

2022 SKCA 7
, at paragraph
22
).
Denunciatory
sentences express a “collective statement that the offender’s conduct should be
punished for encroaching on our society’s basic code of values” (
see
R.
v. M. (C.A.)
,
1996 CanLII 230 (SCC)
,
[1996] 1 S.C.R. 500
, at paragraph
81
).
As
a result, though I “
can accord significant weight to other
factors” I “cannot give them precedence or equivalency” (
see
R. v.
Bertrand Marchand
,
2023 SCC 26
, at paragraph
28
).

[
5
]     I must also
consider the numerous other offences committed by
Mr.
Rowsell.  For instance, threatening a police officer is always a serious
offence.  In this case, it is aggravated by the racial slurs uttered against
that officer by Mr. Rowsell during the threats (see
section 718.2
(a)(i) of the
Criminal
Code
, which indicates that “evidence that [an] offence was motivated
by…hate based upon race…shall be deemed to be [an] aggravating circumstance”).

[6]     It
has been suggested that the “the justification for treating prejudicial
offending as an aggravating factor in sentencing can be grouped into three
broad categories: (1) the elevated harm to the victim, the group to which the
victim belongs or is perceived to belong, and the wider community; (2) the
elevated culpability of the perpetrator; and (3) denunciation of the offending
as immoral and contrary to values of society” (see
Prejudice and
Discrimination as Aggravating Factors in Sentencing
, Sentencing Advisory
Council, February, 2024, at page 9).

[7]     Finally, I must
consider Mr. Rowsell’s personal circumstances.  He has suffered from
significant alcohol addiction.  He has an extensive criminal record that includes
numerous offences of violence, and he has been unwilling to comply with court orders.

[8]     The pre-sentence
report sets out Mr. Rowsell’s history of violence against other intimate
partners, in the following manner (a
t pages 8, 9 and 10):

The
accused then entered into another roughly five-year relationship with Ms. A.
Two children, presently 13 and 12 were born as a result. Mr. Rowsell states
that his drinking and that jealousy by both were issues in the first couple of
years of the relationship when they lived in Ontario. He explains that he was
working a lot, 'playing in the bands' and drinking on the weekends (he does not
feel that this was excessive or out of control) and that 'she didn't like it'.
He states that they argued frequently and that he was subsequently convicted of
assaulting her (he later served 30 days for this incident.).

In
2005 the accused entered into a relationship with Ms. B…Mr. Rowsell states that
he was involved 'off and on' with her for roughly four years. They have one
child, presently six years of age. Again the accused did not discuss this
relationship in any detail. He did state that they argued frequently, that they
were both 'heavy drinkers' and that there were a number of separations and
reconciliations. The accused was convicted of assaulting Ms. B and later
convicted of uttering threats against her. He has not had any contact with her
or his child in several years.

[From
a Pre-Sentence Report for a prior offence, which was quoted in the report filed
in this case.] The accused had been involved in a relationship with Ms. C (the
victim in the matters presently before the Court) for roughly one year prior to
his incarceration in late 2011…Mr. Rowsell expresses mixed feelings and some
ambiguity and confusion about this relationship. He admits that there were some
arguments but no violence before the matter presently before the Court. He
indicates that the relationship was 'convenient' as he was not allowed in his
home in Deer Lake (due to an undertaking), so he spent a lot of time at her
home. He feels that she had a problem with prescription drug abuse. At the same
time, he relates he continues to have “feelings for her”.

[9]     In summary, Mr.
Rowsell is an extremely violent individual who constitutes a significant danger
to the public, to the police, and to intimate female partners.  He refuses to
comply with court orders.  Anything but a lengthy period of incarceration would
be disproportionate and woefully inadequate.  It would fail to contribute to
maintaining a safe society.

[10]   Finally, though
the use of incarceration is at times criticized, it will serve at least one
useful purpose in this case: it will prevent Mr. Rowsell from assaulting
another member of the public, including any other women, while he is
incarcerated.  This is no small thing, and it is consistent with
the
fundamental purpose of sentencing: “to protect society and to contribute…to the
maintenance of a just, peaceful and safe society” (see
section 718
of the
Criminal
Code
).  As the Supreme Court of Canada has recently pointed out, “having
regard to the protection of society as a factor aligns with the purposes,
objectives, and principles of sentencing” (
see
R. v. J.W.
,

2025 SCC 16
, at paragraph
60
).  I would suggest that the protection of our
society and the maintenance of safety, includes the protection and safety of
specific groups, such as female intimate partners.

My Decision:

[11]
Based
upon the circumstances of the offences and the circumstances of the offender, I
have concluded that an appropriate overall sentence in this case is a period of
6 years of incarceration. I have concluded that this is an appropriate overall
sentence because of the number of offences committed by Mr. Rowsell, his
criminal record, the seriousness of the offences committed by him, the harm he
caused to Ms. X, and the racial element involved in his threats to Constable
Anjum.

[12]   Let me explain my
reasons for imposing this sentence in greater detail by commencing with a
review of the circumstances of the offences committed by Mr. Roswell.

The Circumstances of the Offences
Involving Ms. X:

[13]
The evidence presented at the trial established that Ms. X and Mr.

Rowsell
had started dating in the summer of 2024.  On October 30, 2024, Ms. X was
residing at
Mr.
Rowsell’s
residence.

[
14
]   On October 30, 2024, Ms. X went to Mr. Rowsell’s residence to
pick up some of her personal belongings.  She had fled from the residence the
night before, after an incident occurred that caused Mr.
Rowsell
to become very angry and upset.

[15]   When
Ms.
X arrived the next morning, Mr. Rowsell was still very angry and upset.  He was
yelling at her and calling her names.  He told her to hurry up and to get the
“fuck out”.  He suggested that the only way she was leaving was in a “body
bag”.

[16]
Ms.
X went into the main bedroom to get her belongings. Mr. Rowsell “grabbed” her
by her hair and threw her on the bed.

[17]
Mr.
Rowsell was “pacing” back and forth in front of the bedroom’s door.  Ms. X was
sitting on the bed.  Mr. Rowsell entered the bedroom and pulled her shoes off.  He
struck her in the head with his fist and with one of her shoes and said: “You
are not fucking going anywhere”.

[18]   Ms. X wanted to leave, but Mr.
Rowsell was blocking the door. He is considerably bigger than she is.  Ms. X
was “begging” to leave, but Mr. Rowsell pushed her back on to the bed.

[19]   Mr. Rowsell subsequently struck
Ms. X on top of her head with a golf club, cutting her head.  Blood was pouring
out of her head, down on to her face.

[20
]
Ms. X was scared.  She got up on the bed
and took a screen out of a window in the bedroom.  She opened the window and
climbed out.  She did not have any shoes on.  Mr. Rowsell grabbed her foot, but
she was able to escape.  She went to the police station.

At the Police Station:

[21]   The first officer that had
contact with Ms. X described her having a cut on the top of her head.  Another
officer described it as an “open laceration”.  That officer described blood
“running down” on to Ms. X’s face.  A third officer described the top of Ms.
X’s head as being “slit”.  The officer testified that Ms. X appeared to “be in
shock”.

[22]   The police took photographs of
Ms. X while she was at the police station.   Amongst other things, these
photographs show Ms. X’s face, the top of Ms. X’s head and her legs.  Blood can
be seen in her hair and on her cheek.  There is also a bruise on her cheek
below the blood.  There is blood throughout her hair.  She does not have any
shoes on.  She has a bruise on her right knee. She has only one legging on.

[23]   The photograph of the top of
her head shows a clear red mark:

The Medical Report:

[24]   After speaking to the police,
Ms. X was taken to the hospital. The medical reports entered at the trial indicate
that she had “a laceration to her scalp”, and “bruising and swelling to [her]
face”.  One staple was applied to the laceration.

Factual
Conclusions:

[25]   Based upon the evidence
presented at the trial, I concluded as follows (at paragraph 116):

-On
October 30, 2024, Ms. X went to Mr. Rowsell’s residence to retrieve her
belongings;

-Mr.
Rowsell allowed Ms. X to enter the residence, but began to threaten that she
would be leaving in a body bag;

- Mr.
Rowsell grabbed Ms. X by her hair and threw her on to the bed;

- Ms. X
begged to leave, but Mr. Rowsell pushed her onto the bed;

-Mr.
Rowsell removed Ms. X’s shoes and struck her with his fist and one of her
shoes; and

-Mr.
Rowsell struck Ms. X on the top of her head with a golf club, causing the
injuries referred to earlier.

[26]   Having reached these factual
conclusions, I applied them to the charges laid against Mr. Roswell in the
following manner (at paragraphs 118 to 122):

Assault
(two counts):

Mr.
Rowsell assaulted Ms. X by pulling her hair, by pushing her on to the bed, by
striking her with his fist, and by striking her with one of her shoes, causing
bruising to her face.

Aggravated
Assault:

Mr.
Rowsell assaulted Ms. X by striking on the top of her head with a golf club.
This caused a break in the skin on top of her head and a serious injury; i.e.,
a wound.

Unlawful
Confinement:

Ms. X
begged to leave the residence, but Mr. Rowsell pushed her onto the bed and
forced her to remain in the bedroom through his assaults upon her and by
threatening her.  This constituted an unlawful confinement.

Uttering a
Threat:

Mr.
Rowsell threatened Ms. X by stating that she would be leaving in a body bag and
pulling on the television cord in a manner that suggested he was going to choke
her with it.  Mr. Rowsell uttered and conveyed a threat to cause harm to Ms. X
that he intended for her to take seriously and to intimidate her.

Breach of
a Release Order (two counts):

Mr.
Rowsell breached the release order he was bound with by failing to keep the
peace and be of good behavior and by consuming alcohol.

The Other Offences:

[27]   The other offences committed by
Mr.
Rowsell were committed on April 6, and September 17, 2024.

April 6, 2024 (
sections 264.1(1)
(a) [3
counts] and 430(1)(c)):

[28]
On April 6, 2024, the
police responded to a complaint from Deer Lake of an aggressive male saying
that he was going to “kill everyone”.

[29]   The police responded to the street
from which the complaint originated and upon which Mr. Rowsell resides.  They saw
Mr. Rowsell walking down that street.  [30] The police spoke to the complainant,
Ms. Melissa Hutchings, who told them that Mr. Rowsell was severely intoxicated
and said that he was going to kill her and everyone on the street.  She
indicated that Mr. Rowsell was yelling and hitting his house and screaming: “You
bitch, you bitch, I’ll fucking kill you, you bitch”.

[31]   Mr. Nathan Ellsworth, Ms.
Hutchings’ partner, told the police that Mr. Rowsell had “pulled his pants
down.  His penis and ass were out, and he was bending over and was spreading
his cheeks towards people on the road”.

[32]   The police arrested Mr. Rowsell.  Constable
Anjum advised Mr. Rowsell that he was under arrest for uttering threats.  He asked
him if he understood.  Mr. Rowsell replied: “Fuck you, N…”.

[33]   Constable Anjum informed Mr.
Rowsell of his right to counsel.  He asked Mr. Rowsell if understood. Mr.
Rowsell said: “Fuck you, N…”.  He told Constable Anjum to “get the white guy to
do it”.  Mr. Rowsell continued to use the “N word” and called Constable
Anjum a “Paki, a cocksucker, a bitch, a cunt, and a Jew”.  He told Constable
Anjum that he was going to stab him.

[34]   The police drove Mr. Rowsell to the
police station. During the drive, Mr. Rowsell was continuously hitting his head
off the silent patrolman and spitting all over the inside of the police vehicle.

[35]   At the police station, Constable
Anjum read the police caution to Mr. Rowsell. When he asked Mr. Rowsell if he
understood, Mr. Rowsell told him to “suck [his] big white cock”.

[36]   The police drove Mr. Rowsell to the
lock-up in Corner Brook.  During the drive, Mr. Rowsell continued to say to
Constable Anjum: “Fuck you, N…”.  He threatened to shoot Constable Anjum.  He
suggested that the people living on the street upon which he was arrested,
should “find a new address” as he would “be out tomorrow”.

[37]   Finally, Mr. Rowsell asked
Constable Anjum why he did not work at Tim Hortons.  He said to Constable Anjum
that he looked “like a terrorist”.

[38]   Based upon the circumstances,
including the words used and the repeated use of them by Mr. Rowsell, I am
satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the threats were racially motivated.
Mr. Rowsell’s comments went well beyond threatening a police officer because of
their position or actions.

[39]
In
R. v. Woodward
,

2011 BCCA 251
, the British Columbia Court of Appeal considered section
718(2)(a)(i) and noted that the conduct it deems to be aggravating, “is
antithetical to our collective beliefs” (at paragraph 27):

Section
718(2)(a)(i) reflects the fact that Canadians take pride in being members of a
pluralistic, multicultural society, in which every individual is entitled to
respect.  Not only do we abhor violence, we particularly abhor it being
gratuitously directed at someone solely because of his or her personal
characteristics, such as race, religion, sexual orientation, etc.  Such conduct
is antithetical to our collective beliefs.

September 17, 2024 (
section 145(5)
):

[40]   Mr. Rowsell was released.  The
release order prohibited him from having any “contact or communication” with
Ms. Hutchings and/or Mr. Ellsworth.

[41]   On September 17, 2024, the police
received a complaint that Mr. Rowsell was creating a disturbance on the street
upon which he resides.  The police responded and learned that Mr. Rowsell was
continuously outside his residence, yelling and pointing at Ms. Hutchings’ and
Mr. Ellsworth’s residence.

[42]   The police arrested Mr. Rowsell.
One of the arresting officers was
Constable Anjum.  This
time, Mr. Rowsell asked him how to “spell N…”

Mr. Roswell’s Personal Circumstances:

[43]
In
R. v. Branton
,
2013 NLCA 61
,
the Court of Appeal indicated that a "fit sentence" is one "that
takes account of the circumstances of the offences and the offender" (at
paragraph 56).  However, as pointed out by the Manitoba Court of Appeal, “the
accused’s personal factors, while important, take on a reduced role where the
principles of denunciation and deterrence are paramount” (
see
R.
v. Arac
,
2025 MBCA 54
,
at
paragraph
15
).

[44]   Mr. Roswell is fifty-one years of
age.  He was born at Corner Brook.  He is the younger of two children born to
Gloria Drover of Corner Brook, but was placed in a foster home when he was two
weeks old and was subsequently adopted.

[45]   The pre-sentence report indicates
that Mr. Rowsell “did not know the identity of his biological father until he
was an adult”.  He has had minimal contact with his biological mother.

[46]   Mr. Rowsell told the author of the
pre-sentence report that that alcohol use began to be a problem for him in his
youth.  He stated that his “alcohol use over the years has continued to be the
main contributing factor to all of his issues and that he recognizes that he
should abstain completely from any further use.  He noted that he was able to
abstain from alcohol use for 5 years and 11 months until he relapsed in April
2024.  He recalled that, at that time, he had a bad day at work and decided to have
a drink to relax; thinking that he could handle doing so.  His problematic use
of alcohol spiraled from there and was an issue up until his current remand.  He
stated that he was disappointed in himself for the relapse”.

Whatever weight is or is not given to an addiction in imposing sentence, the

consideration of the latter factor and Mr. Rowsell would have been aware of the
effect of alcohol on his continuous resort to violence.  As a result, his
addiction does not lessen his moral culpability.

The Relevance of an Addiction in
Sentencing:

[54]   A drug or alcohol

see
R.
v. Sheppard

(1997),
1997 CanLII 14629 (NL CA)
,
147 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 304 (N.L.C.A.)
),
particularly when an offender commits an isolated criminal act to satisfy the
addiction and he or she has illustrated a commitment to rehabilitation.
In those cases, the Court may resort to a community based sanction, depending
upon the seriousness of the offence, in the hope that rehabilitation will be
successful (see for instance,
R. v. Reid
,
[2003]
P.E.I.J. No. 118 (C.A.)
).

[55]   However, as pointed out by Judge
Harris noted in
R. v. Maher
,
[2024] N.J. No. 194 (P.C.)
, “[w]hile
a drug or alcohol addiction can be mitigating, the mitigation is
significantly less or non-existent when the offence is a serious one or the

.  R. v. Breen

(1982),

1982 CanLII 3889 (NL CA)
,
37 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 472 (N.L.C.A.)
noted at paragraph
7
that while the
effects of alcohol or drugs can be considered mitigating factors in sentence,
“that consideration is normally confined to cases where the actions of a person
are completely out of character.  Thus, lenient treatment may be justified
in anticipation of rehabilitation” (at paragraph 26).

In

The Principles of Sentencing:

[66]
In
R. v. Knott
,
2012 SCC 42
,
it was held that "the purpose and principles of sentencing set out in the
Criminal Code

are meant to take into account the correctional imperative of sentence
individualization" (at paragraph 47). In
R. v. Suter
,
2028
SCC 34
, the Supreme Court of Canada indicated that sentencing “is a highly
individualized process.  A delicate balancing of the various sentencing
principles and objectives is called for, in line with the overriding principle
that a ‘sentence must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the
degree of responsibility of the offender’” (at paragraph 4).  Similarly,
in
R.
v. Boudreault
,
2018 SCC 58
,
the Supreme Court of Canada indicated that “sentencing is first and foremost an
individualized exercise, which balances the various goals of sentencing, while
taking into account the particular circumstances of the offender as well as the
nature and number of his or her crimes” (at paragraph 58).

The Fundamental
Purpose of Sentencing:

[67]
Section 718
of the
Criminal Code

states that the fundamental purpose of sentencing "is to contribute...to
respect for the law and the maintenance of a just, peaceful, and safe
society."  This is to be achieved by imposing sentences that have,
among other objectives, the objectives of:

-denouncing unlawful conduct and the harm
done to victims or to the community;

-separating
offenders from society, where necessary;

-specific
and general deterrence;

-rehabilitation;
and

-the promoting of a "sense of
responsibility in offenders, and acknowledgment of the harm done to victims or
to the community."

[68
]

In
R. v. Butler
,
2019 NLCA 21
, the Court of Appeal indicated that
the “fundamental purpose of sentencing is to protect society and contribute to
respect for the law and the maintenance of a just, peaceful and safe society
(section 718 of the
Code
).  This goal is meant to be achieved by
application of the principles and objectives set out in the
Code
and
interpreted in the jurisprudence to the facts and circumstances of each case”
(at paragraph 35).

[69]
In
R. v.
Hills
,
2023 SCC 2
, the Supreme Court held that “[t]o assist in
evaluating what constitutes a just and appropriate punishment in a given case,
Parliament enacted
s. 718
of the
Criminal Code
… Proper consideration is
to be given to various objectives such as denunciation, deterrence,
rehabilitation, providing reparations for harm done to victims, promoting a
sense of responsibility and, when necessary, separating offenders from society.
No sentencing objective should be applied to the exclusion of all others.
Courts should also consider any aggravating and mitigating circumstances
relating to the offence or to the offender” (at paragraph 54).

Mitigating and
Aggravating Factors:

[70
]

Section 718.2
(a) of the
Criminal Code

indicates that a "sentence should be increased or reduced to account for
any relevant aggravating or mitigating circumstances relating to the offence or
the offender."
In
R. v. Briand
,
2010 NLCA 67 (CanLII)
,
[2010] N.J. No. 339 (C.A.)
,
the Court of Appeal stressed the importance of considering an offender's
personal circumstances in applying section 718.2(a) of the
Criminal Code
.

The Fundamental
Principle of Sentencing:

[71
]

Section 718.1
of the
Criminal Code

sets out the “fundamental principle” of sentencing.  It states as follows:

A
sentence imposed must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the
degree of responsibility of the offender.

[72]   This is the
only principle of sentencing in the
Criminal Code
that contains as its
heading the words: “Fundamental principle” (
see
R.
v. Parranto
,
2021 SCC 46
,
at
paragraph
10
).  Thus, its importance cannot be overstated.  As indicated by the
Supreme Court of Canada, “whatever weight a judge may wish to accord to the
objectives [of sentencing as set out in
sections 718
to
718.2
of the
Criminal
Code
], the resulting sentence
must
respect the fundamental principle
of proportionality” (
see
R. v. Nasogaluak
,
2010 SCC 6 (CanLII)
,
[2010] 1 S.C.R. 206
,
at paragraph
40
, Supreme Court’s emphasis).

[73]   Similarly,

in
Friesen
, the Supreme Court of Canada indicated
that
“[a]ll sentencing starts with the principle that sentences must be
proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of
the offender. The principle of proportionality has long been central to
Canadian sentencing…and is now codified as the ‘fundamental principle’ of
sentencing in
s. 718.1
of the
Criminal Code
”

(at paragraph 30).

[74]
In
Parranto
,
the Supreme Court of Canada pointed out that “[u]nlike other principles of
sentencing set out in the
Criminal Code
, proportionality stands alone
following the heading ‘Fundamental principle’ (
s. 718.1
).  Accordingly, ‘[a]ll
sentencing starts with the principle that sentences must be proportionate to
the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender’…The
principles of parity and individualization, while important, are secondary
principles” (at paragraph 10).  As a result, in imposing sentence, I must
concentrate on the gravity of the offences and Mr. Smith’s moral culpability.

Gravity
of the Offences:

[75]   The
Supreme Court indicated
in
Hills
that “[t]he ‘gravity of the
offence’ refers to the seriousness of the offence in a general sense and is
reflected in the potential penalty imposed by Parliament and in any specific
features of the commission of the crime…The gravity of the offence should be
measured by taking into account the consequences of the offender’s actions on
victims and public safety, and the physical and psychological harms that flowed
from the offence” (at paragraph 58).

[76]
In
R. v.
Jimmy
,

2023 SKCA 28
, the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal
suggested that “
three main considerations define the gravity of an
offence” (at paragraph 39):

(a)
its nature and comparative seriousness, (b) the circumstances of its
commission, and (c) the harm caused by it.

This
Case:

[77
]
Mr. Roswell committed a number of grave offences.  He
assaulted a woman with whom he had an intimate relationship, numerous times,
including striking her on the top of her head with a golf club, while bound by
a release order.  He threatened a police officer, motivated at least in part,
by the officer’s race and/or ethnic background.  He threatened his neighbors
and failed to comply with a court order designed to protect them from him.

An
Offender’s Moral Culpability:

[78]   The
Supreme Court
held in
Hills
that “[t]he offender’s moral
culpability or degree of responsibility should be measured by gauging the
essential substantive elements of the offence including the offence’s
mens
rea
, the offender’s conduct in the commission of the offence, the
offender’s motive for committing the offence, and aspects of the offender’s
background that increase or decrease the offender’s individual responsibility
for the crime” (at paragraph 58).

This
Case:

[79]   Mr. Roswell’s moral culpability is at
a very high level.  His offences did involve negligence or carelessness.  He
intentionally committed numerous offences, including striking Ms. X with a golf
club on the top of her head.  Mr. Rowsell would have known the potential harm
he was subjecting her to. The fact that he had consumed alcohol does not, based
upon his background, offer any mitigation or lessen his moral culpability for
the offences committed by him.

Parity:

[80]   As “a general
proposition, like cases should be treated alike in terms of sentencing.  This
is known as the principle of parity” (
see
R.
v. Sousa
,
2023 ONCA 100
, at paragraph
20
).
However, “[p]arity does not mean uniformity in sentencing. It does not shift
the court’s focus away from proportionality, but instead serves to inform the
proportionality principle by helping to define what is a proportionate
sentence…the principle of parity does not detract from the need for sentences
to be individualized. Differing personal circumstances between offenders can
justify differing sentences for similar offences” (
see
Jimmy
, at
paragraphs
53 and 54
).

[81]
Section 718.2
(b)
of the
Criminal Code

indicates that “a sentence should be similar to
sentences imposed on similar offenders for similar offences committed in
similar circumstances”.
In
R. v. Pearce
,
2021 ONCA 239
, it was
indicated that “[t]
his
guiding principle preserves fairness in sentencing by promoting the equal
treatment of offenders according to law” (at paragraph 17).  Therefore, a
“sentence is proportionate when it reconciles the individual offender’s
circumstances and the relative parity of sentences imposed for similar offences
committed in similar circumstances” (
see
R. v. Le
,
2023 ONCA 79
,
at paragraph
194
). However, it has also been pointed out that “while parity
must be considered, it is not an overriding principle; the sentencing process
is by its very nature, an individualized process” (
see
R. v. Phiri
,

2023 ABCA 18
, at paragraph
23
).

Separation of
Offenders from Society:

[82]
Section 718
(c) of
the
Criminal Code
indicates that one of the objectives of sentencing in
Canada is "to separate offenders from society, where necessary”.  In this
case, Mr. Rowsell’s history of violence and his repeated failures to comply
with court orders, establishes that he must be separated from society.

The Least
Restrictive Sanction that is Reasonable:

[83]
Section 718.2
(d)
of the
Criminal Code
indicates that “an offender should not be deprived
of liberty, if less restrictive sanctions may be appropriate in the
circumstances”. Section 718.2(e) of the
Criminal Code
states that:

…all
available sanctions, other than imprisonment, that are reasonable in the
circumstances and consistent with the harm done to victims or to the community
should be considered for all offenders, with particular attention to the
circumstances of Aboriginal offenders.

[84]   These provisions
were
considered by the Ontario Court of Appeal in
R. v. Romano
,

2021 ONCA 211
.  The Court of Appeal indicated that “a sentencing judge is
required to consider all sanctions apart from incarceration and impose
imprisonment only when there is no other reasonable punishment…It follows that
where imprisonment is required, the term should be as short as is reasonable
given the circumstances” (at paragraph 64).

[85]   However, though these
provisions speak of restraint,
section 718.2
(e) also states that such restraint
must be “consistent with the harm done to victims or to the community”.  An
assault against an intimate partner is an offence against that victim, but also
an offence against the community because of the long term and significant
societal harm such offences cause.

Denunciation:

[86]
In
Hills
,
the Supreme Court of Canada indicated that “[d]enunciation and deterrence, both
general and specific, are valid sentencing principles…Denunciatory sentences
express a ‘collective statement that the offender’s conduct should be punished
for encroaching on our society’s basic code of values’…and the need for
denunciation is closely tied to the gravity of the offence” (at paragraph 139).

The
Criminal
Code
’s Intimate Violence Sentencing Provisions:

[87]
In
Bear
, the
Saskatchewan Court of Appeal has pointed out that “Parliament saw fit to
legislate how judges should approach sentencing for crimes involving intimate
partners” (see at paragraph 23).

[88]
Section 718.201
of
the
Criminal Code
indicates that a court that “imposes sentence in
respect of an offence that involved the abuse of an intimate partner shall

[89]   In addition,
section
718.2
(a)(ii) of the

states that if an offence involves the
abuse of an intimate partner, this is to be considered an aggravating factor in

court that imposes sentence shall also take into consideration the following principles

(a)
a sentence should be increased or reduced for any relevant aggravating or

limiting the generality of the forgoing,

(ii) evidence that the offender, in committing the

shall be deemed to be an
aggravating factor.

In
R. v.
Cunningham
,
2023 ONCA 36
, the

Within the criminal justice system, Parliament
introduced Bill C-75 in 2019.  A key aspect of the Bill was a focus on intimate

the expansion of
s. 718.2
(a)(ii) of the
Criminal Code
, R.S.C. 1985,
c. C-46
, directing that the commission
of an offence involving abuse of an intimate partner must be considered an

the
Code,
which provides discretion to sentencing judges to

out
in
Cunningham
that that there has been “an increase in
society’s awareness of the prevalence of domestic violence and the evils it

[92]   Finally, the
Ontario
Court of Appeal suggested
in
Cunningham

that
the changes to the
Criminal Code

enacted by Parliament

“clearly
supports enhanced penalties for perpetrators of domestic violence and

[93]   Despite
Mr.
Roswell’s

not isolated acts of violence.  Mr.
Roswell
has
a long standing history of violence, and he refuses to comply with court

The
Use of Sentencing Precedents:

[111]

In

Friesen
, the Supreme Court pointed out that it “has repeatedly
held that sentencing ranges and starting points are guidelines, not hard and
fast rules” (at paragraph 37).  However, the Supreme Court also indicated
in
Friesen

that a

proportionate sentence “for a given offender and offence cannot be deduced from
first principles; instead, judges calibrate the demands of proportionality by
reference to the sentences imposed in other cases. Sentencing precedents
reflect the range of factual situations in the world and the plurality of
judicial perspectives. Precedents embody the collective experience and wisdom
of the judiciary. They are the practical expression of both parity and
proportionality” (at paragraph 39).  Of course, they only reflect the
collective wisdom of those sentencing decisions placed in writing or
transcribed from oral decisions.  Since very few sentencing decisions are
placed in writing, it becomes difficult if not impossible to know what the real
range is, unless one has been prescribed by the Court of Appeal.  Finally,
sentencing precedents are not carved in stone.  Our recognition of the harmful
effects of certain crimes changes and evolves overtime.
Friesen
reflects
this process in relation to sexual offences against children.
Cunningham

reflects it in relation to offences committed against intimate partners.

[112] Sentencing
precedents are welcome and useful. Counsel are encouraged to file and rely upon
them.  However, they must be properly applied by the judiciary.

[113] Sentencing
involves great discretion, based upon the specific circumstances involved.  As
set out in
section 718.3 (1)
of the
Criminal Code
: “Where an enactment
prescribes different degrees or kinds of punishment in respect of an offence,
the punishment to be imposed is, subject to the limitations prescribed in the
enactment, in the discretion of the court that convicts a person who commits
the offence”.

[114] Many of the
precedents filed here are of limited use because though they involve aggravated
assaults, they do not involve the commission of that offence in circumstances
in which there was an extended period of violence committed against an intimate
partner who was unlawfully confined by an offender with a long history of
violence.  Those that involved the commission of an aggravated assault upon an
intimate partner (
O’Flaherty
,

White
,
and
King
)
involved single incidents and they occurred before the enactment of
An
Act to amend the Criminal Code, the Youth Criminal Justice Act and other Acts
and to make consequential amendments to other Acts
,
S.C. 2019
.  This latter factor is important.  Let
me explain.

[115]
In
R.
v. Squires
,
2012 NLCA 20
,
the Court of Appeal considered the former
section 718.2
(a)(ii)
of the
Criminal Code
(“evidence
that the offender, in committing the offence, abused the offender's spouse or
common law partner" shall "be deemed to be an aggravating
circumstance").  In that case, the offender was convicted of a number
of offences involving a woman he was involved in an intimate relationship with.
The trial judge, in imposing sentence, relied upon the nature of the
relationship as an aggravating factor pursuant to
section 718.2
(a)(ii) of
the
Criminal Code
.

[116]
On appeal, the Court of Appeal held that he had erred in doing so because in
its view the "rationale underlying
section 718.2
(a)(ii) is directed
to the vulnerability and dependency, particularly from an emotional, financial
and psychological perspective, presumed to arise from the domestic relationship
between married or common-law spouses. The relevance of this factor is
heightened where physical or psychological abuse results in a sense of
powerlessness making escape or leaving the relationship difficult" (at paragraph
31).

[117] The law of
sentencing in relation to assaults in intimate relationships has changed
dramatically since the Court of Appeal rendered its
decision in
Squires
.

[118]
First of all,
section 718.2
(a)(ii) was amended post-
Squires
as
a result of
An Act to amend the Criminal Code, the Youth Criminal
Justice Act and other Acts and to make consequential amendments to other Acts
.
At the time
Squires
was decided, the application
of
section 718.2
(a)(ii)
of the
Criminal Code
was
limited to assaults against a “spouse or common-law partner”.  It
presently applies to an “intimate partner”.  In addition, at the
time
Squires
was decided, Parliament had not
enacted
section 718.201
of
the
Criminal Code
, which indicates that a court that “imposes
sentence in respect of an offence that involved the abuse of an intimate
partner shall consider the increased vulnerability of female persons who are
victims”.

[119] As a result,
sentencing precedents for offences involving violence in an intimate
relationship that occurred prior to the enact of
An Act to amend the
Criminal Code, the Youth Criminal Justice Act and other Acts and to make
consequential amendments to other Acts
, must be cautiously applied.

[120] Finally, as

noted in
Cunningham
,
as a society, we have come to realize the seriousness of intimate partner
violence, its prevalence in our society, and its heinous and at times, life
threatening effects.  This has caused an increase in the severity of sentences
impose for such offences, as illustrated by the sentencing precedents referred
to and by the Ontario Court of Appeal’s
comments in
Cunningham

(see paragraph
52
).

The
Statutory Regime:

[
121]

The “starting point in any consideration of the imposition of criminal
punishment must be that it is imposed for the offence for which the offender
has been convicted” (see
Elias v The Queen
[2013] HCA 31, at
paragraph 26).

[122] T
he
Supreme Court of Canada has indicated that
in “exercising discretion
in sentencing, a sentencing judge must consider the current values of society,
as reflected by the maximum sentences in force for the offence…Sentences must
not only be proportionate to an individual’s culpability (Cr. C.,
s. 718.1
),
they must serve sentencing’s fundamental purpose of maintaining a ‘just,
peaceful and safe society’” (
see
R. v. Archambault
,
2024 SCC 35
,
at paragraph
294
).

[123]
The maximum penalty which can be imposed for the aggravated assault offence, is
a period of fourteen years of imprisonment. However, because Mr. Rowsell has
been convicted of an
indictable offence in which violence was
used against an intimate partner and because he has been previously convicted
of an offence in which violence was used against an intimate partner, I can
impose a period of life imprisonment.
Section 718.3(8)
(d) of the
Criminal
Code
creates this possibility
:

If
an accused is convicted of an indictable offence in the commission of which
violence was used, threatened or attempted against an intimate partner and the
accused has been previously convicted of an offence in the commission of which
violence was used, threatened or attempted against an intimate partner, the
court may impose a term of imprisonment that is more than the maximum term of
imprisonment provided for that offence but not more than

(d) life,
if the maximum term of imprisonment for the offence is 14 years or more and up
to imprisonment for life.

[124] Section 718.3(8)(d)
is an example of how Parliament has consistently amended the
Criminal Code

to reflect the seriousness of offences involving violence in intimate
relationships and to allow judges to impose condign sentences when appropriate.

The

a general sense and is reflected in the potential penalty imposed by Parliament
and in any specific features of the commission of the crime (
R. v. Hamilton

(2004),
2004 CanLII 5549 (ON CA)
,
72 O.R. (3d) 1 (C.A.)
, at para.
90
). The gravity of the offence should
be measured by taking into account the consequences of the offender's actions
on victims and public safety, and the physical and psychological harms that
flowed from the offence. In some cases where there is bias, prejudice or
hatred, the motivation of the offender may also be relevant (see
s. 718.2
(a)(i)
of the
Criminal Code
). The offender's moral culpability or degree of
responsibility should be measured by gauging the essential substantive elements
of the offence including the offence's
mens rea
, the offender's conduct
in the commission of the offence, the offender's motive for committing the
offence, and aspects of the offender's background that increase or decrease the

, at para.
91
;
Boudreault
,
at para.
68

Ipeelee

Concurrent or
Consecutive?

[191]

In
Hutchings
, the Court of Appeal indicated
that after determining the individual sentences that should be imposed, the
next step is to determine if the individual sentences imposed should be served
on a concurrent or consecutive basis. [192] The Court of Appeal suggested
in
Hutchings

that the individual
sentences imposed "should
presumptively
be imposed
consecutively" (my emphasis, at paragraph 20).
In

R. v. B.H
.
,
2022 NLCA 54
, the Court of Appeal indicated that it
“is well established that sentences should be consecutive unless there is a
valid reason for making them concurrent…A valid reason would include multiple
convictions arising out of a single criminal venture, or as a method of
achieving proper totality” (at paragraph 14).

[193]  Periods of
imprisonment imposed for breach of court order offences should generally be
served consecutively so as to reflect the separate interests offended and
to
ensure that the offender does not get a “free ride” for having committed them.

In

R. v. Tuglavina
,

2020 NLCA 30
, the Court of Appeal noted that it had earlier ruled that periods
of imprisonment for the offence of breach of probation “will generally result
in a sentence to be served consecutively”.  The Court of Appeal concluded that
“[t]o impose a concurrent sentence for a breach of probation without
explanation as to why it was appropriate in these circumstances and to depart
from the generally accepted principle of imposing a consecutive sentence
constitutes an error” (at paragraph 40).

[194] The
Criminal
Code
indicates that when imposing more than one
sentence,
a court “shall consider directing” that they be served consecutively in the
following circumstances (see
section 7
18.3
(4)
):

(a) that
the term of imprisonment that it imposes be served consecutively to a sentence
of imprisonment to which the accused is subject at the time of sentencing; and

(b) that the terms of imprisonment
that it imposes at the same time for more than one offence be served
consecutively, including when

(i) the offences do not arise out of
the same event or series of events,

(ii) one of the offences was committed
while the accused was on judicial interim release, including pending the
determination of an appeal, or

(iii) one of the offences was
committed while the accused was fleeing from a peace officer.

This Case:

[195] In this case, the offences
committed by Mr. Rowsell against Ms. X all occurred in the same time frame.
However, they involved very distinct and separate delicts.  For instance, Mr.
Rowsell threatened her. He assaulted her.  He assaulted her again.  He confined
her.  He threatened her again.  He then struck her with the golf club.  I must
be careful to avoid structuring the sentences in a manner that ignores the reality
of the overall circumstances of the commission of these crimes by Mr. Rowsell and
ensure that he does get the benefit of a free ride in relation to any of them.

[196] For instance, if I make the
sentences imposed for the violent offences committed against Ms. X, all
concurrent, then it would be as if the only offence committed by Mr. Rowsell in
relation to Ms. X was the aggravated assault.  This would be contrary to the
reality of what occurred, and the degree of harm caused to her beyond that
single offence. I could increase the sentence imposed for the aggravated
assault offence to reflect the other assaults and threats, but this would be
contrary to the principle of imposing an appropriate sentence for each offence
and involve the premature application of the totality principle.  Having said
this, though the three assaults were separate incidents that should result in
consecutive sentences, they occurred during the unlawful confinement, which
should result in a concurrent sentence for the latter offence.

[197] As can be seen, we start off
with a presumption that the periods of imprisonment imposed will be
consecutive, followed by an analysis to determine whether any should be
concurrent.  This analysis is based upon an uncertain and difficult standard to
apply.  However, this is not a real problem because when a judge imposes
multiple sentences, whether concurrent or consecutive, they must take one last
look to ensure that the overall sentence imposed is proportionate to the
overall offending by that offender.  In other words, that the total sentence
imposed is not too harsh nor too lenient.

[198] In relation to the offences
committed on April 6 and September 17, 2024, these were committed on separate
dates and are not related to each other.  Several offences were committed on
April 6, 2024, but they are also distinct delicts in which consecutive
sentences should be imposed.

unlawful

uttering
a threat

6. for the
uttering
a threat

one month of incarceration, consecutive;

uttering
a threat
offence against
Constable

a period of six months of
incarceration, consecutive;

13. for the breach of a release order

[200] Adopting this approach would
result in a total period of eight years, six months, and fifteen days of
imprisonment being imposed.  Is this a proportionate sentence?

The Totality
Principle of Sentencing:

[201]

In
Hutchings
, the Court of Appeal
indicated that
section 718.2
(c) of the
Criminal Code

"requires consideration of whether a combined sentence is unduly long or
harsh 'where consecutive sentences are imposed'. On its plain reading, this
means that considerations of totality are engaged in all cases involving the
potential imposition of consecutive sentences" (at paragraph 67).

[202]

Subsequently,
i
n
R. v. O'Keefe
,
2018
NLCA 11
, the Court of Appeal noted that the
totality principle in sentencing "evolved from the principles set out in

sections 718.1
and
718.2
of the
Criminal Code
,
which require a sentence to be 'proportionate to the gravity of the offence and
the degree of responsibility of the offender' and 'where consecutive offences
are imposed, the combined sentence should not be unduly long or harsh'"
(at paragraph 28).

[203]
Considering the circumstances of the offences and Mr. Rowsell’s personal
circumstances, I conclude that the imposition of a period of period of eight
years, six months, and fifteen days of imprisonment would be unduly long.  I am
satisfied that the imposition of a period of six years of imprisonment would
constitute a proportionate overall sentence.

[204]
This is achieved by making
all of the sentences
concurrent, except for the ones imposed for the aggravated assault, the assault
upon Ms. X in which Mr. Rowsell pulled her hair, and the offence of having
uttered a threat against her.
